title: Solid-State Transformers and the Medium-Voltage Hall Edge — Megmeet’s Competitive Position
topic: Who is positioned to win the medium-voltage-to-800 V DC hall-edge block, measured by the service-voltage class each vendor has actually specified and by what has actually been sold — and where Megmeet stands in it

scope.rationale: The hall-edge block cut as a single layer rather than as the four-layer roster of the 2026-09-08 edition. Eighteen dossiers: the company the report is written for (megmeet); the four venture solid-state-transformer vendors (heron-power, amperesand, dg-matrix, novos-power — the last three of which entered coverage after that edition); the Asia-headquartered vendors with a published medium-voltage or 800 V DC conversion product (sungrow, zhonhen, sinexcel, delta-electronics, liteon); and the incumbents that have declared an 800 V DC position at or above the block (abb, ge-vernova, eaton, schneider-electric, vertiv, hitachi-energy, siemens-energy) plus the silicon layer that gates all of them (infineon). vicor, flex, huawei-digital-power, oracle and nvidia are covered but out of scope — the first three sit at layers this cut does not score, and the last two are buyers and architecture-setters rather than competitors in it.

gaps: Megmeet's solid-state transformer has no disclosed service-voltage class anywhere in its 81 pinned sources, which now include every filing and investor-relations record from September 2024 to August 2026 — the single largest collection gap in this report, and the one that keeps it out of the hall-edge comparison.
Heron Power, Amperesand, DG Matrix and Novos Power are private and carry no normalized revenue, so the scale chart omits the four companies whose products are closest to the block being scored.
Amperesand publishes no datasheet: per-unit MW, dimensions, DC output voltage and input class all rest on third-party reporting.
Novos Power's record is a website, two pitch-competition wins and one analyst citation. No datasheet, patent, paper, funding round or customer is visible, so it is named rather than scored.

No vendor in this scope publishes an overload curve, a part-load efficiency curve, a mean-time-between-failures figure for a complete medium-voltage converter, or a spares and service model. The layer's operations-and-maintenance record is empty.

Siemens Energy carries no solid-state-transformer programme in its pinned sources; the development work reported elsewhere in the trade record sits with a different corporate entity and is therefore outside this coverage.

Eaton's ownership of solid-state-transformer intellectual property is carried in its dossier as an assessment of its acquisition record rather than as a cited product fact, so it appears in this report's analysis section and not in the class table.
No company in the scope discloses a US utility qualification, an approved-equipment-list entry, or a named host utility for a medium-voltage converter.

bluf: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: The hall-edge contest is not being decided on efficiency — every serious vendor claims 98.5% and none publishes the boundary — but on two things the corpus can actually measure: the service-voltage class a vendor has specified, and whether anything has been sold. On the first test the field inverts. The only covered vendor whose filing describes an MV-to-800 V DC solid-state transformer as supplying the market, Sungrow, is specified at 10–13.8 kV and stops there; the two most completely specified 34.5 kV-class products belong to the two smallest balance sheets in this report, neither of which has shipped a unit; the only orderable solid-state medium-voltage product from an incumbent is a UPS, not a transformer; and the one venture vendor actually shipping hardware is shipping a 480 V AC skid, not the medium-voltage unit its marketing rates at 15 MW. Megmeet sits outside this table on the one axis that defines it: its revised dossier — eighty-one sources, including every filing and investor-relations record from September 2024 to August 2026 — still discloses no service-voltage class for its solid-state transformer, which the company itself describes as under research and does not expect to sell in volume for two to three years. Its disclosed position is the rack and the sidecar, where it is measurably growing, and its exposure is that the block above it consolidates before its own converter has a class to quote.

keyJudgments.text: We assess the service-voltage class, not efficiency, is the discriminator in this layer, and that on that test the commercial leader and the specification leader are different companies. Sungrow's EnerNeo is specified 10 kV–13.8 kV medium-voltage AC in, 800 V DC out, 3 MW standard and 1.5–4.5 MW configurable at 98.5% system efficiency [c:c26], and its H1 2026 interim describes the product as launched and supplying the market [c:c25]. Heron Link is specified to connect directly to 34.5 kV at 4.2 MW and over 98.5% [c:c10], with thirty 140 kW cells ten in series per phase and an integrated disconnect rated 40 kA at 34.5 kV [c:c9] — and has not shipped. The class that hyperscale campuses actually take is the class the shipping product cannot serve.

We assess DG Matrix's shipping product is not the product its medium-voltage marketing describes, and that the company's own datasheet is the evidence. The Interport Flex Series 400 kVA specification sheet rates the AC port at 400–480 VAC three-phase and the DC port at 300–850 VDC with a peak efficiency of 96–97% [c:c19] — a low-voltage skid two to three points below the platform's headline figure — while the medium-voltage Interport Cell Series that would transform 12–34.5 kV AC to high-voltage DC is described on the data-centre page rather than on a datasheet [c:c20]. The May 2026 reveal into the NVIDIA MGX ecosystem [c:c21] and the Infineon silicon-carbide supply agreement [c:c22] are real; neither is a medium-voltage unit in the field.

We assess Megmeet is the only company in this report whose solid-state transformer carries no disclosed service-voltage class, and that this is a collection fact rather than an inference. The revised dossier searched the FY2025 annual report [c:c51], the H1 2026 interim [c:c3], the HKEX application proof [c:c52] and the 2024–2026 investor-relations records: the converter is described only as taking grid high-voltage input to 800 V DC, as under R&D, with efficiency above 98.5% stated as expected [c:c3]. One press report gives a 10 kV domestic and 35 kV overseas development plan and attributes it to the May 2026 earnings call [c:c47]; the exchange-filed record of that call describes the SST as in pre-research and contains no kV figure [c:c48]. Its disclosed medium-voltage-adjacent hardware is the sidecar, which converts a building's existing 380–480 VAC — not medium voltage — to 800 V DC at over 1 MW per rack [c:c1], and the 800 V / 570 kW side rack [c:c4]. Until a class is published, the correct cell for Megmeet in every table in this report is 'undisclosed'.

We assess Megmeet's disclosed evidence strengthened exactly where a filing can measure it and stayed silent exactly where one cannot — and that its rack position is a qualified third source, not a number two. The H1 2026 interim reports the power-products group growing 60.92% to RMB 1.841 billion, the only one of the company's three largest segments whose gross margin expanded, and states that Megmeet is one of NVIDIA's designated recommended data-centre power suppliers [c:c3]; the company's reply to the exchange's inquiry defines that as a place on the list NVIDIA recommends to its downstream customers [c:c58], and NVIDIA's own post lists it among power-system components [c:c59]. The company told investors it was late on GB200 and won limited orders there before winning GB300 batch orders [c:c50]. Soochow expects it to become NVIDIA's third NVL72 PSU source after Delta and LITEON [c:c53], TrendForce says its share will take time to build [c:c55], and the contemporaneous supplier account names LITEON as the second supplier [c:c7]. The trade story that Megmeet displaced LITEON at number two traces to an early-2025 piece that attributes it to market rumour [c:c54] and has no supporting source.

We assess the venture set is separated by certification distance rather than by topology, and that none of the four has closed it. Heron has selected a 286,000 sq ft first factory for up to 10,000 units a year [c:c11] and added a USD 60 million credit facility in September 2026 [c:c12]; Amperesand's platform is built on 3.3 kV Wolfspeed full-bridge modules [c:c16] and was shown at PCIM Europe 2026 as a modular medium-voltage unit [c:c17] after an USD 80 million Series A [c:c18]; DG Matrix's datasheet states 'Designed for Compliance to' rather than a listing [c:c19]; and Novos Power's entire product record is a company page claiming a Variable Airgap Solid State Transformer on 13–48 kV utility feeds [c:c23] plus one analyst citation [c:c24]. Four topologies, four funding positions, and no listed medium-voltage unit among them.

We assess the incumbents have converged on one hedge — own the block around the converter, defer the converter — and that the only orderable solid-state medium-voltage product in the set is not a transformer. ABB's HiPerGuard is a static medium-voltage UPS at 2.5 MW per unit to 25 MW paralleled, 98% efficiency, with voltage classes now extended by a 34.5 kV direct-grid-connect class [c:c36][c:c37]. GE Vernova publishes 800 V DC AI-factory reference designs rather than a dated product [c:c38]; Eaton published an 800 V DC reference architecture at OCP 2025 [c:c39] after a July 2025 NVIDIA collaboration [c:c40]; Schneider's 800 V DC contribution is a sidecar and a set of reference designs [c:c41]; Vertiv declared engineering readiness rather than a medium-voltage product [c:c42]; Hitachi Energy co-designed a grid-to-rack architecture [c:c43] while committing USD 1 billion of US transformer manufacturing including a USD 457 million Virginia plant [c:c44].

We assess whole-company scale is the wrong ranking for this layer and that the corpus demonstrates it in both directions. Siemens Energy carries a EUR 162 billion group backlog [c:c45] and Infineon publishes a solid-state-transformer position inside a power-semiconductor franchise [c:c46], yet neither sells a hall-edge converter; Zhonhen's Panama-800VDC lineage is a transformer-rectifier architecture converting 10 kV in one stage [c:c28] and its H1 2026 interim carries no order, backlog or customer for it [c:c29]; Sinexcel's management records state that its AI-data-centre critical-power products are samples in development with formal sales not yet realised [c:c31], and the string '800V' does not appear in its 212-page interim [c:c30]. The two most specified 34.5 kV-class products in this report belong to the two smallest balance sheets in it.

We assess Megmeet's competitive risk in this report is not Delta and not LITEON, but the possibility that the block above the rack consolidates before its own converter has a class to quote. Delta publishes the deepest 800 V DC architecture in the set including a medium-voltage front end [c:c32] and is the named primary beneficiary of a 2026 volume-shipment call [c:c33]; LITEON has committed to a McKinney, Texas plant [c:c34] and showed a liquid-cooled 800 V rack at Computex 2026 [c:c35]. Megmeet competes with both at the shelf, where it publishes a 110 kW liquid-cooled MGX shelf [c:c6], a 27.5 kW N+1 shelf [c:c8] and an OCP-stage 800 V DC collaboration [c:c2], and has placed a test lab on US soil [c:c5]; its own website also describes a 35,000 sq ft manufacturing base in Richardson, Texas [c:c56], matched by a Texas licensing record for a Megmeet fit-out there [c:c57], which its HKEX application proof does not list among its manufacturing bases [c:c52]. None of that is a hall-edge position.

sections.title: What changed since the morning edition of 23 September
ps: **This edition supersedes `sst-hall-edge-block--competitive--2026-09-23`.** It re-pins three dossiers revised the same afternoon — Megmeet to profileVersion 8, Delta Electronics to 6 and LITEON to 7 — and changes only what those revisions change. Every other row, figure and citation is carried unchanged.

**Megmeet's class is still undisclosed, and the negative is now wide.** The morning edition rested it on thirty-eight dossier sources. The revised dossier searched every filing and investor-relations record from September 2024 to August 2026 and both company websites, and found no kV figure; it also shows the efficiency wording narrowing from an unqualified figure in the April annual report [c:c51] to 'expected' in the June and August documents [c:c52][c:c3]. A single press report of a 10 kV / 35 kV plan now enters the record as a bounded lead, not a fact [c:c47][c:c48].

**One error in the morning edition is corrected.** It called power products 'the only segment with an expanding gross margin'. Three of Megmeet's six segments expanded in H1 2026; power products was the only one of the three largest to do so [c:c3]. The correction runs through key judgement 4 and the Megmeet section.

**The number-two claim is closed rather than contested.** The morning edition set a trade account against a supplier account. The revised dossiers trace the account to market rumour [c:c54] and record 2026 research placing Megmeet as a prospective third source [c:c53][c:c55] — the Delta and LITEON dossiers were corrected the same day.

**Two new facts about Megmeet's footprint and timing.** The company's website describes a Richardson, Texas manufacturing base that its HKEX proof does not list [c:c56][c:c52], and the company now dates its own SST sales two to three years out [c:c49].

sections.title: What this edition adds to the 8 September edition
ps: **This report builds on `aidc-power-conversion--competitive--2026-09-08` and does not supersede it.** That edition cut the covered roster by layer — silicon, the rack, the sidecar and hall-edge block, the facility and grid tier — and scored fifteen companies across all four. This one takes a single layer, the medium-voltage-to-800 V DC hall-edge block, and re-cuts it on the axis that edition could not: **the service-voltage class each vendor has actually specified**. The two reports answer different questions and both remain current.

**Three dossiers landed after that edition and they change the layer's shape.** Amperesand moved to profileVersion 2, and DG Matrix and Novos Power entered coverage for the first time, all on 19 September 2026. The hall-edge set the September edition scored as three names (Zhonhen, Sungrow, Sinexcel, with Delta reaching down from the rack) is now a set of nine once the venture SST vendors and the incumbents' declared programmes are counted at the same layer.

**Where this edition contradicts the earlier one, it is on DG Matrix and it is a correction of placement, not of judgement.** The September edition did not scope DG Matrix. Its dossier now establishes that the product on the market is the Interport Flex Series — a low-voltage skid whose own specification sheet states a 400–480 VAC port and 96–97% peak efficiency [c:c19] — while the medium-voltage Cell Series that would compete at the hall edge is described on the data-centre page without a datasheet [c:c20]. Any reading that places DG Matrix among the shipping medium-voltage vendors is placing the wrong product.

**Where it extends the earlier one, it is on the class question.** The September edition's final indicator was 'a second covered vendor stating in a filing that a 34.5 kV-class or MV-direct SST is supplying the market'. This edition makes the first half of that indicator measurable: it records, per vendor, what class has been specified, on whose authority, and whether anything at that class has been sold. The answer is that **no covered vendor has both**.

**What has not changed is the disclosure asymmetry the earlier edition named.** No company in this scope discloses an audited AI-data-centre power-conversion revenue line. Every share figure in circulation for this layer is a trade or brokerage estimate produced by a party that sells research or sells equipment, and this report states none of them as fact.

sections.title: Whole-company scale — and why it does not rank this layer
sections.unit: USD millions, latest full fiscal year, normalized
sections.intro: Fourteen of the eighteen companies in scope carry a normalized revenue figure. **The four that do not are the four venture SST vendors — Heron Power, Amperesand, DG Matrix and Novos Power — and they are precisely the companies whose products are specified closest to the block this report is about.** That is the finding, not a gap in the chart.
sections.note: Denominator: whole-company revenue for the latest full fiscal year in each dossier's normalized-KPI overlay, converted at the rate each dossier records. Fiscal years are not aligned — Infineon's and Siemens Energy's FY2025 ended 30 September 2025, Hitachi Energy's ended 31 March 2026, the rest are calendar 2025 — and no company here discloses an AI-data-centre power-conversion revenue line, so this is a scale indicator and not a position in the contest. Read the ordering, not the gaps.

sections.title: Where Megmeet actually stands in this layer
ps: **The honest statement of Megmeet's position at the hall edge is that it does not have one yet, and that this is a disclosure fact before it is a capability judgement.** The company publishes a chain that runs from an AC compensator through backup shelves and a solid-state transformer to a megawatt-class sidecar and on to the point of load. Everything in that chain below the converter is specified, priced into product pages and shipping. The converter itself is described by output and efficiency and by nothing else. A buyer's electrical engineer asks the input class in the first ten minutes, and the published record has no answer.

**What Megmeet does hold is the layer where money is moving first, and the interim measures it.** The power-products group grew 60.92% to RMB 1.841 billion in H1 2026 and was the only one of the company's three largest segments whose gross margin expanded. That is the rack and the sidecar — Options A and B in the deployment staging the industry is building to — and it is a real, growing, margin-positive business that two of the three largest incumbents in this report do not have at all.

**The company has now dated the option itself.** In its August 2026 investor-relations record Megmeet said SST demand will not ramp quickly for one to two years and that its sales for the next two to three years will come from its existing product matrix [c:c49]. Its commercial account of the rack is similarly modest: late on GB200 with limited orders, then GB300 batch orders contributing from the first quarter of 2026 [c:c50]. Read together, those two statements place Megmeet's hall-edge converter in the later part of the decade on the company's own word — not on an analyst's.

**The competitive risk is structural rather than commercial.** If the hall-edge block consolidates around a small number of certified medium-voltage converters before Megmeet publishes a class, the company's addressable content per megawatt is capped at the rack while the conversion stage above it is captured by someone else. That is the same arithmetic the facility incumbents face from below, arriving at Megmeet from above. It is not a Delta problem or a LITEON problem: both of those are shelf competitors, and Megmeet is measurably competitive with them.

**Against the venture set the comparison runs the other way and favours Megmeet.** Heron, Amperesand, DG Matrix and Novos have, between them, no revenue, no listed medium-voltage unit and one shipped product that is not a medium-voltage unit. Megmeet has a manufacturing base, a filed financial record, named Western network-power customers of long standing, and a test facility on US soil. What it lacks is the one specification they lead with. In a procurement conversation those are not symmetric weaknesses — a specification can be published in a quarter; a manufacturing record cannot be acquired in one.

**The single most useful thing that could change this assessment is a published service-voltage class.** Until then every comparison in this report places Megmeet in the rack layer with an undisclosed option on the layer above, and any statement that puts it in the hall-edge contest is an assertion the record does not support.

indicators.confirms: The incumbents' hedge is to defer the converter; the first dated product ends the deferral and closes the window the venture set is funded against

limitations: This report is built from covered dossiers only and cites their sources verbatim. It does not re-research, and it is therefore silent on anything that entered the public record after each pinned dossier's lastUpdated date — the oldest pin here is 4 September 2026 and the newest 23 September 2026.

No company in this scope discloses an audited AI-data-centre power-conversion revenue line. Every market-share figure in circulation for this layer originates with a research house, a brokerage or a vendor, and none is stated as fact here.
'Undisclosed' in the class table is a statement about the pinned sources, not about the vendor's engineering. A company may hold a class it has not published, and several almost certainly do.

Efficiency figures are not comparable across rows. Every vendor in this report claims 98.5% or better, none publishes the measurement boundary, and the one datasheet figure in the set — DG Matrix's 96–97% peak — is two to three points below its own platform claim precisely because it is a datasheet rather than a marketing page.

The four venture SST vendors carry no normalized-KPI figure, so the scale chart cannot include them. Heron Power, Amperesand, DG Matrix and Novos Power are private, disclose no revenue, and are compared here on specification and certification distance instead.

Amperesand's unit rating and input class rest on a supplier case study and trade-show reporting rather than on a company datasheet, because the company publishes none. The figures are attributed to those parties in the rows that use them.

Megmeet's items rest on Chinese-language exchange filings read in the original — the H1 2026 interim, the FY2025 annual report and the 2024–2026 investor-relations records — plus the English HKEX application proof. The single most consequential fact drawn from them here is a negative — that no service-voltage class, order figure, customer name or AI-data-centre revenue line appears in any of them — and a negative finding, however wide the search, is inherently weaker evidence than a positive one.

Zhonhen's Panama architecture is a transformer-rectifier lineup and is scored as one. It is in scope because buyers and trade coverage place it against solid-state transformers, not because it is one.

ABB's HiPerGuard is a static medium-voltage UPS, not a medium-voltage-to-800 V DC converter. It appears in the class table because it is the only orderable solid-state medium-voltage product in the scope, and the distinction is stated in its row rather than left to the reader.

vicor, huawei-digital-power, flex, oracle and nvidia are covered but out of scope: the first three sit at layers this report does not score, and the last two are buyers and architecture-setters rather than competitors in it.
